title: Negatives on the line, and graphs: dots and lines
summary: Put positive and negative numbers on a line to add, subtract and compare them, then explore graphs: dots, lines, routes, degree and map colouring.

problems.prompt: A rhythm repeats every 5 beats: clap, clap, rest, clap, rest. Over 15 beats (3 full repeats), what fraction of the beats are rests?
explanation: One repeat of 5 beats has 3 claps and 2 rests, so 2 out of 5 beats are rests in each cycle.
That same 2-out-of-5 fraction holds for all 3 repeats: 2 x 3 is 6 rests out of 5 x 3, which is 15 beats.
6/15 shrinks to 2/5, matching the fraction in just one cycle.
problems.useAgain: when a repeating pattern's fraction of rests stays the same no matter how many times the pattern repeats.
hints: Work out the fraction of rests in just one 5-beat cycle first.
Check that the same fraction holds once the cycle repeats 3 times.
problems.socraticHint: If one repeat of the pattern has a fixed fraction of rests, does repeating it more times ever change that fraction?

variant.prompt: A rhythm repeats every 4 beats: clap, rest, rest, clap. Over 12 beats (3 full repeats), what fraction of the beats are rests?

problems.prompt: Drummer A claps on beats 1, 3, 5 and 7 of an 8-beat bar. Drummer B claps on beats 1, 2, 5 and 6. On what fraction of the 8 beats does EXACTLY ONE of the two drummers clap (not both, not neither)?
explanation: Go beat by beat: beat 1 and beat 5 have both drummers clapping, and beat 4 and beat 8 have neither.
The remaining beats, 2, 3, 6 and 7, each have exactly one drummer clapping.
That is 4 beats out of 8, which is 4/8, or 1/2.
problems.useAgain: when you need the fraction of beats where exactly one of two patterns is active, not where both or neither are.
hints: First find the beats where both clap, and the beats where neither claps.
Whatever is left over is where exactly one drummer clapped.
problems.socraticHint: Every beat falls into one of three groups: both clap, neither claps, or exactly one claps. Do those three groups have to add up to all 8 beats?

variant.prompt: Drummer A claps on beats 1, 2, 4 and 6 of an 8-beat bar. Drummer B claps on beats 2, 3, 5 and 7. On what fraction of the 8 beats does EXACTLY ONE of the two drummers clap?

problems.prompt: A bar has 6 beats. Clap on every beat except beat 2. What fraction of the beats did you clap?
explanation: You clapped on 5 of the 6 beats, so that is 5/6.
5 and 6 share no number bigger than 1 that divides them both evenly, so 5/6 is already the simplest slice size.
problems.useAgain: when a clap pattern skips only one beat in the whole bar.
hints: Count how many beats you skipped, that is often faster than counting the ones you clapped.
Check whether the top and the bottom of that fraction share any common factor before shrinking.
problems.socraticHint: Which is faster to count here, the beats you clapped, or the one beat you did not?

variant.prompt: A bar has 6 beats. Clap on every beat except beats 2 and 5. What fraction of the beats did you clap?

problems.prompt: A bar has 8 beats. Clap on every beat except beats 3 and 6. What fraction of the beats did you clap?
explanation: You clapped on 6 of the 8 beats, so that is 6/8.
Same slice: 6 and 8 both divide evenly by 2, so shrink both.
6/8 shrinks to 3/4.
problems.useAgain: when a clap pattern skips two beats out of eight and the leftover fraction can be shrunk.
hints: Count how many beats you skipped first, then subtract that from the total.
Check whether the top and bottom of the resulting fraction share a common factor.
problems.socraticHint: If the two beats you skipped were sitting right next to each other instead of spread apart, would the fraction of beats you clapped be any different?

variant.prompt: A bar has 8 beats. Clap on every beat except beats 1, 4, 5 and 8. What fraction of the beats did you clap?

problems.prompt: A bar has 6 beats. Clap on beats 2, 4 and 6. What fraction of the beats did you clap?
explanation: You clapped on 3 of the 6 beats, so that is 3/6.
Same slice: 3 and 6 both divide evenly by 3, so shrink both.
3/6 shrinks to 1/2.
problems.useAgain: when a fraction of beats out of 6 can be shrunk down to halves.
hints: Write the claps as a fraction of the total beats first.
3 out of 6 can be written with smaller numbers.
problems.socraticHint: Is there a pattern to which beats you clapped that might let you picture the fraction without counting one by one?

variant.prompt: A bar has 6 beats. Clap on beats 1, 3, 4 and 6. What fraction of the beats did you clap?

problems.prompt: A 4-beat bar contains a dotted half note worth 3 beats, with one more note filling the rest of the bar. What fraction of the bar's beats does that remaining note take up?
explanation: The whole bar is 4 beats, and the dotted half note takes up 3 of them.
Whatever note fills the rest of the bar takes 4 minus 3, which is 1 beat.
1 beat out of 4 total beats is 1/4.
problems.useAgain: when one note's beat value is given and you need the fraction the leftover note fills in the bar.
hints: Subtract the known note's beats from the bar's total beats first.
Write the leftover beats as a fraction of the whole bar.
problems.socraticHint: If one note already uses most of the bar, does the leftover note have to be a small fraction or a big one?

variant.prompt: A 6-beat bar contains a dotted half note worth 3 beats and a half note worth 2 beats, with one more short note filling the rest of the bar. What fraction of the bar's beats does that remaining short note take up?

problems.prompt: A bar has 6 beats. You play on beats 1, 3, 4 and 6, and rest on the others. What fraction of the beats are rests?
explanation: You played on 4 of the 6 beats, so you rested on the other 2 beats, beats 2 and 5.
That is 2 rests out of 6 beats, or 2/6.
Same slice: 2 and 6 both divide evenly by 2, so shrink both. 2/6 shrinks to 1/3.
problems.useAgain: when you need the fraction of a bar that is rests instead of the fraction that is played.
hints: Figure out which beats were rests first, not which beats were played.
Write the rests as a fraction of the total beats, then see if it can be shrunk.
problems.socraticHint: If you already knew the fraction of beats that were played, how would that help you find the fraction that were rests, without recounting the whole bar?

variant.prompt: A bar has 6 beats. You play on beats 1, 4 and 6, and rest on the others. What fraction of the beats are rests?

problems.prompt: A bar has 8 beats. You play on beats 2, 3, 4, 6, 7 and 8, and rest on the others. What fraction of the beats are rests?
explanation: You played on 6 of the 8 beats, so you rested on the other 2 beats, beats 1 and 5.
That is 2 rests out of 8 beats, or 2/8.
Same slice: 2 and 8 both divide evenly by 2, so shrink both. 2/8 shrinks to 1/4.
problems.useAgain: when the rests in a bar are scattered instead of all bunched together, but the fraction still shrinks.
hints: Figure out which beats were rests first, not which beats were played.
Write the rests as a fraction of the total beats, then see if it can be shrunk.
problems.socraticHint: Does it matter whether the beats you rest on sit next to each other or are scattered across the bar, when all you need is how many there are?

variant.prompt: A bar has 8 beats. You play on beats 1, 3, 5 and 7, and rest on the others. What fraction of the beats are rests?

problem.prompt: A rectangular garden is 12 meters by 18 meters. A gardener lays a path exactly one meter wide all the way around the inside edge, using square tiles one meter on each side, and leaves a rectangle of grass in the middle. How many tiles does the path use?
explanation: Do not count the border tiles one at a time. Work out the whole garden first: 12 x 18 is 216 square meters.
The path takes one meter off every side. So the grass in the middle is 10 by 16, which is 160 square meters.
The path is whatever is left when the grass is taken away: 216 minus 160 is 56 tiles.
problem.useAgain: when you need the size of a border, a frame or a shell, and the whole and the inside are both easy to work out.
hints: Find the area of the whole garden, then the area of the grass that is left in the middle.
A border one meter wide takes one meter off each side, so the grass is two meters shorter in each direction, not one.
problem.socraticHint: If you walked the path once around, how many tiles would you step on along the long side, and would the corner tiles get counted twice that way?

variant.prompt: A rectangular garden is 10 meters by 15 meters. A path exactly one meter wide runs all the way around the inside edge, made of square tiles one meter on each side, with grass in the middle. How many tiles does the path use?

problems.prompt: The temperature starts at -4 degrees. It drops 6 degrees, then rises 9 degrees. What is the final temperature?
explanation: Number line: start at -4 and move 6 steps left for the drop: -4 minus 6 is -10.
Then move 9 steps right for the rise: -10 plus 9 is -1.
The final temperature is -1 degrees, still below zero even after the rise.
problems.useAgain: when a temperature or amount changes twice in a row, once down and once up, starting from a negative number.
hints: Handle the drop first, completely, before applying the rise.
A rise after a drop does not always bring you back above zero.
problems.socraticHint: Does the temperature end up warmer than where it started, colder, or exactly the same?

variant.prompt: The temperature starts at -7 degrees. It drops 5 degrees, then rises 9 degrees. What is the final temperature?

problems.prompt: A diver is at -18 meters. She rises to a depth that is exactly halfway between her current depth and the surface (0 meters). What is her new depth?
explanation: Number line: the surface is 0, and she starts at -18 meters.
Halfway between -18 and 0 is their average: (-18 plus 0) divided by 2, which is -9.
Her new depth is -9 meters.
problems.useAgain: when you need the exact midpoint between a negative position and zero, or between two negative positions.
hints: Halfway between two numbers is their sum divided by 2.
Halfway to the surface from -18 is not the same as rising 18 meters.
problems.socraticHint: If she rose exactly half of the 18 meters, where would she end up?

variant.prompt: A hiker is at -24 meters below base camp. He climbs to a point exactly halfway between his current elevation and base camp (0 meters). What is his new elevation?

problems.prompt:
Wesley computed -3 minus -8 like this:
Line 1: Subtracting a negative number is the same as adding its positive.
Line 2: So -3 minus -8 becomes -3 minus 8.
Line 3: -3 minus 8 is -11.
Line 4: So -3 minus -8 is -11.
Which line is wrong?
explanation: Line 2 is wrong: subtracting a negative flips to adding, so -3 minus -8 should become -3 plus 8, not -3 minus 8.
Line 1 correctly states the rule, but line 2 does not apply it, it drops the sign instead of flipping it.
Line 3's subtraction is done correctly for the expression it uses, but that is the wrong expression.
-3 plus 8 is 5, so -3 minus -8 is really 5.
problems.useAgain: when a subtraction has two minus signs in a row and one of them needs to flip to a plus.
hints: Two minus signs in a row are not the same as one. What does subtracting a negative turn into?
Rewrite the expression yourself using that flip, then compare your rewritten expression to the one used in the solution.
problems.socraticHint: On the number line, does taking away a debt of 8 move you further left, or does it move you to the right?

variant.prompt:
Priya computed -6 minus -10 like this:
Line 1: Subtracting a negative number is the same as adding its positive.
Line 2: So -6 minus -10 becomes -6 minus 10.
Line 3: -6 minus 10 is -16.
Line 4: So -6 minus -10 is -16.
Which line is wrong?

problems.prompt: You start at some unknown number on the number line. You move 5 steps right, then 8 steps left, and land on -2. What number did you start at?
explanation: Work backwards: start at the ending point, -2, and undo the moves in reverse order.
Undo the 8 steps left by moving 8 steps right: -2 plus 8 is 6.
Undo the 5 steps right by moving 5 steps left: 6 minus 5 is 1, the starting number.
problems.useAgain: when you know where a sequence of moves along the number line ends up, and need to find where it started.
hints: Undo the moves in reverse order, right becomes left and left becomes right.
Start from the final position, -2, and work backwards one move at a time.
problems.socraticHint: If you undo a move to the left, which direction do you move instead?

variant.prompt: You start at some unknown number. You move 7 steps right, then 10 steps left, and land on -1. What number did you start at?

problems.prompt: Which of these equals 3 - (-5)?
explanation: Number line: subtracting a negative number flips the direction, so it moves you to the right instead of the left, the same as adding.
Instead of moving 5 steps left, which plain subtraction would do, subtracting -5 moves 5 steps right.
Start at 3 and move 5 steps right: 3 plus 5 is 8.
problems.useAgain: when you subtract a negative number and need to know which direction to move on the line.
hints: Subtracting a negative number does not move you left, it moves you right, the same as adding.
Turn 3 - (-5) into 3 + 5 before you work it out.
problems.socraticHint: Look at 3 - (-5) sitting next to 3 + 5. Why might a double negative and a plain positive end up pointing the exact same direction?

variant.prompt: Which of these equals 4 - (-3)?

problems.prompt: Which of these is the distance between -6 and 4 on the number line?
explanation: Number line: distance is how many steps apart two points are, no matter which direction you count.
From -6 to 0 is 6 steps, then from 0 to 4 is 4 more steps.
6 plus 4 is 10, so -6 and 4 are 10 steps apart.
problems.useAgain: when you need how far apart two numbers are on the line, not just which one is bigger.
hints: Count the steps from the smaller number up to zero first, then from zero up to the bigger number.
Add those two step counts together.
problems.socraticHint: Is the distance between two points on the line ever a negative number, no matter which two points you pick?

variant.prompt: Which of these is the distance between -9 and 2 on the number line?

problems.prompt: The temperature overnight drops to -7 degrees. By midday it rises to 5 degrees. Which of these is how many degrees the temperature rose?
explanation: Number line: the rise is the distance from -7 up to 5.
From -7 up to 0 is 7 steps, then from 0 up to 5 is 5 more steps.
7 plus 5 is 12, so the temperature rose 12 degrees.
problems.useAgain: when a temperature or score moves from below zero to above zero and you need the total change.
hints: Split the rise into two parts: from -7 up to zero, and from zero up to 5.
Add those two parts together for the total rise.
problems.socraticHint: Is asking how many degrees the temperature rose the same question as asking how far apart -7 and 5 are on the line?

variant.prompt: The temperature overnight drops to -4 degrees. By midday it rises to 9 degrees. Which of these is how many degrees the temperature rose?

problems.prompt: Put these four elevations in order from deepest to shallowest: -120 meters, -85 meters, -45 meters, -200 meters.
explanation: Number line: farther left on the line means a smaller, more negative number, and a more negative elevation means deeper.
Placing all four on the line: -200 sits farthest left, then -120, then -85, then -45 sits closest to zero.
Deepest to shallowest is -200, -120, -85, -45 meters.
problems.useAgain: when comparing several negative numbers where more negative means farther down or farther behind, not less important.
hints: Picture all four numbers on the number line and see which sits farthest to the left.
The number farthest to the left is the smallest one, and here that means the deepest.
problems.socraticHint: Between two negative elevations, does 'deeper' mean the smaller number or the bigger number?

variant.prompt: Put these four elevations in order from deepest to shallowest: -60 meters, -220 meters, -140 meters, -15 meters.

steps.title: Graphs: dots, lines, routes and colors

problems.prompt: A graph in math is not a bar chart. It is just dots, called vertices, connected by lines, called edges. Here is a graph: dot A connects to dot B, dot B connects to dot C, and dot A does not connect to dot C. How many edges does this graph have?
explanation: Dots and lines: draw a dot for A, a dot for B and a dot for C before you count anything.
Draw a line between A and B, since they connect. Draw a line between B and C, since they connect too.
A and C do not connect, so there is no line between them.
Counting the lines you actually drew, there are 2 edges in this graph.
problems.useAgain: when a word problem describes things connected to other things, and drawing dots and lines first makes it easier to see.
hints: Draw one dot for each thing mentioned before you draw any lines.
Only draw a line where the problem actually says two dots connect.
problems.socraticHint: If dot A and dot C are never mentioned as connecting, should a line ever get drawn between them?

variant.prompt: Here is a graph: dot X connects to dot Y, dot Y connects to dot Z, dot Z connects to dot X. How many edges does this graph have?

problems.prompt: Six towns are connected by roads, drawn as dots and lines. Town P connects to Q and R. Town Q connects to P and S. Town R connects to P, S and T. Town S connects to Q, R and U. Town T connects to R and U. Town U connects to S and T. Starting at P, what is the fewest roads you must drive to reach U?
explanation: Count the steps: count how many roads you drive, not the straight-line distance between the towns.
From P, you can reach Q or R in 1 road.
From there, R also reaches T and S in 1 more road, so those towns are 2 roads from P.
From S or T, one more road reaches U, so U is 3 roads from P. No shorter route exists, since P does not connect straight to S, T or U.
problems.useAgain: when several towns, rooms or dots connect to each other and you need the fewest steps between two of them, not the shortest straight line.
hints: List every town reachable from P in exactly 1 road first.
Then use those towns to find everything reachable with one more road, and keep going a step at a time until you reach U.
problems.socraticHint: Why can't you just count the towns named between P and U, the way you might count stops on a straight road trip?

variant.prompt: Five towns are connected by roads: town M connects to N and O. Town N connects to M and P. Town O connects to M, P and Q. Town P connects to N, O and Q. Town Q connects to O and P. Starting at M, what is the fewest roads you must drive to reach Q?

problems.prompt: A network of dots: dot 1 connects to dots 2 and 3. Dot 2 connects to dots 1 and 4. Dot 3 connects to dots 1, 4 and 5. Dot 4 connects to dots 2, 3 and 6. Dot 5 connects to dots 3 and 6. Dot 6 connects to dots 4 and 5. Starting at dot 1, match each destination dot to the fewest lines you must cross to reach it.
explanation: Count the steps: build up distances one line at a time, using dots you have already reached.
From dot 1, dots 2 and 3 are reachable in 1 line.
From dot 2, dot 4 is reachable in 1 more line, so dot 4 is 2 lines from dot 1.
From dot 3, dots 4 and 5 are reachable in 1 more line too, putting dot 5 at 2 lines from dot 1.
Dot 6 connects to both dot 4 and dot 5, so it is reachable in 1 more line after them. That makes dot 6 exactly 3 lines from dot 1.
problems.useAgain: when you need the fewest lines to reach several different dots from the same starting dot, not just one destination.
hints: Work out everything reachable in 1 line first, then use that to find everything reachable in 2 lines.
A dot might be reachable from more than one direction, but you only need the shortest way to it.
problems.socraticHint: Could a dot ever be reached in two different numbers of steps depending on which path you take, or does only the shortest path count here?

variant.prompt: A network of dots: dot 1 connects to dots 2 and 3. Dot 2 connects to dots 1 and 5. Dot 3 connects to dots 1 and 4. Dot 4 connects to dots 3 and 5. Dot 5 connects to dots 2 and 4. Starting at dot 1, match each destination dot to the fewest lines you must cross to reach it.

problems.prompt: In this graph: A connects to B, A connects to C, A connects to D, and B connects to C. How many lines touch dot A? That number is called its degree.
explanation: Count the lines: the degree of a dot is just how many lines touch it, not how many other dots exist.
Dot A has a line to B, a line to C, and a line to D.
That is 3 lines touching A, so A has a degree of 3.
The line between B and C does not count, since it does not touch A at all.
problems.useAgain: when you need to know how many connections one single dot has, not how far apart two dots are.
hints: Only count lines that actually touch dot A itself.
A line between two other dots that are not A does not add to A's degree.
problems.socraticHint: If a line does not touch dot A at all, should it change A's degree, no matter how important that line looks on the page?

variant.prompt: In this graph: P connects to Q, P connects to R, Q connects to R, and Q connects to S. How many lines touch dot Q?

problems.prompt: In this graph: A connects to B, C, D and E. B also connects to C. D also connects to E. Which dot has the highest degree?
explanation: Count the lines: work out each dot's degree one at a time before comparing them.
A connects to B, C, D and E, four separate lines, so A has degree 4.
B, C, D and E each only connect to A and one other dot, so every one of them has degree 2.
A's degree of 4 is higher than every other dot's degree of 2, so A has the highest degree.
problems.useAgain: when you need to compare several dots' degrees to find which one connects to the most lines.
hints: Work out the degree of every dot first, one at a time, before comparing them.
A dot connected to the most different other dots will have the highest degree.
problems.socraticHint: Between a dot with several separate connections and a dot with only a couple, which one sounds like it would have more lines touching it?

variant.prompt: In this graph: P connects to Q, R, S and T. Q also connects to R. S also connects to T. Which dot has the highest degree?

problems.prompt: A map has three countries that all touch each other: country X touches Y, Y touches Z, and Z touches X. On a map, touching countries cannot share a color. True or false: this map can be colored using only 2 colors.
explanation: Color the map: try to color it with 2 colors and see if it is even possible.
Say X is red. Since Y touches X, Y must be the other color, blue. Since Z touches Y, Z must be red, the opposite of blue.
But Z also touches X, and both X and Z ended up red, the same color. That breaks the rule that touching countries cannot share a color.
No matter which two colors you try first, three countries that all touch each other always end up needing a third color. So 2 colors is never enough for a triangle.
problems.useAgain: when you need to check whether a map or graph can be colored with a certain number of colors so touching parts never match.
hints: Try coloring one country at a time and see where you get stuck.
Notice what happens to the very last country once the first two are already colored.
problems.socraticHint: If you only had two colors to work with, could three countries that all touch each other ever avoid two of them sharing one?

variant.prompt: A map has four countries in a line: country W touches X, X touches Y, and Y touches Z. W does not touch Y or Z, and X does not touch Z. True or false: this map can be colored using only 2 colors.

problems.prompt: A map has four countries: A touches B, A touches C, B touches C, and C touches D. A, B and C all touch each other, and D only touches C. What is the fewest colors needed so no two touching countries share a color?
explanation: Color the map: start with the countries that touch the most others.
A, B and C all touch each other, forming a triangle, so those three need 3 different colors between them, same as any triangle.
D only touches C, so D just needs to avoid C's color. D can reuse whichever color A or B has, since D does not touch either of them.
No fourth color is ever needed, so the fewest colors for the whole map is 3.
problems.useAgain: when part of a map or graph forms a triangle, since a triangle always forces at least 3 colors, and other dots can often reuse colors already used elsewhere.
hints: Find the group of countries that all touch each other first, since that group sets the minimum.
A country that only touches one other country can often reuse a color that is already far away from it.
problems.socraticHint: Does the country that only touches one neighbor ever force the whole map to need a brand new color, or can it always borrow one that is already in play far away?

variant.prompt: A map has five countries: A touches B, A touches C, B touches C, C touches D, and D touches E. What is the fewest colors needed?

problems.prompt: Explain why three countries that all touch each other, forming a triangle on the map, can never be colored with only 2 colors, no matter which 2 colors you pick.

mustMention: first two countries must get different colors
no color is left that differs from both

explanation: Color the map: pick any two of the three countries first, say X and Y. Since they touch, they must already be different colors.
That uses up both of your 2 colors: one on X, the other on Y.
The third country, Z, touches both X and Y, since all three touch each other in a triangle.
Z cannot be the same color as X, and cannot be the same color as Y either. With only 2 colors total, both are already taken, so there is no color left for Z that follows the rule.
problems.useAgain: when you need to explain why a triangle of touching things always forces a third option, not just show one example.
hints: Think about what happens to the first two countries as soon as you know they touch each other.
Ask whether any color is left over once the first two countries have used up both colors.
problems.socraticHint: Showing it happens once is not the same as proving it always happens. What happened to the first two countries here that would happen to any two countries that touch?

problems.prompt:
Construct the perpendicular bisector of segment AB:
1. Open your compass wider than half of AB.
2. Draw an arc above and below AB, centered at A.
3. Keep the same width and draw an arc centered at B, crossing the first two.
4. Draw a line through the two crossing points.
Every point on that line is the same distance from A as from B. A point on the line is 5 cm from A. How far is it from B, in cm?
explanation: The compass width never changed between the arc from A and the arc from B.
That means wherever the two arcs cross, that point is the same distance from both A and B.
The point is 5 cm from A, so it must also be 5 cm from B.
problems.useAgain: when a point sits on a perpendicular bisector, since it must be the exact same distance from both ends of the segment.
hints: What stayed exactly the same width while drawing both arcs?
A point on the bisector is always the same distance from both ends of the segment.
problems.socraticHint: If the compass never changed its width while drawing both arcs, could the crossing point end up closer to one end than the other?

variant.prompt: Using the same construction, a point on the perpendicular bisector is 8 cm from one end of the segment. How far is it from the other end, in cm?

problems.prompt: You roll one die and flip two coins. How many different outcomes are possible in total?
explanation: The die has 6 results, and each coin has 2 results.
Multiply all three counts together: 6 times 2 times 2.
6 times 2 is 12, and 12 times 2 is 24.
problems.useAgain: when three separate random things happen together, and every result of each can pair with every result of the others.
hints: How many results does the die have on its own, and how many does each coin have?
Multiply all three counts together, not just two of them.
problems.socraticHint: Does the second coin's result change anything about the die or the first coin?

variant.prompt: You roll an 8-sided die and flip two coins. How many different outcomes are possible in total?

steps.title: Explain it
steps.prompt: Pick the hardest problem from this week's graph set. Write why your answer must be right, one idea per sentence. Name the idea you used.

steps.title: Explain back
steps.prompt: Say out loud how you found the fewest roads to reach U, as if to your sister.
